title: Fermi's pile comes alive

facts.text: The world's first nuclear reactor was built in a disused squash court under the west stands of Stagg Field, the University of Chicago's abandoned football stadium.

It was a pile of graphite blocks with lumps of uranium metal and uranium oxide set into them, about 20 feet tall. Crews worked round the clock for about two weeks and stopped after the 57th layer on the evening of 1 December 1942.

On the morning of 2 December Enrico Fermi had the control rods pulled out step by step. George Weil stood on the court floor and drew out the last cadmium rod by hand while Fermi read the instruments on the balcony.
Norman Hilberry stood by with an axe, ready to cut a rope that would drop an emergency rod into the pile if anything went wrong.

At 3:25 p.m. Fermi announced that the reaction was self sustaining: the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. It produced about half a watt, enough for a small light bulb. At 3:53 p.m. he ordered the rods back in.

Forty nine people were present. The only woman was the physicist Leona Woods, later Leona Woods Marshall, who had built the pile's boron trifluoride neutron detectors and called out counts during the run.
Eugene Wigner produced a bottle of Chianti, poured into paper cups. The signatures on its label are the only written record of who was there.
Arthur Compton telephoned James Conant with a code made up on the spot: "The Italian navigator has landed in the New World." Conant asked how the natives were. "Very friendly."
The pile ran until early 1943, when it was taken apart and rebuilt outside the city as Chicago Pile 2. Its success opened the way to the plutonium production reactors of the Manhattan Project.

photoNote: Tier: green. Pencil drawing of CP-1 in the squash court under Stagg Field: the stepped stack of graphite bricks, the ladder, the control rod slots, and the steel frame tower at right. Drawn by Melvin A. Miller of Argonne National Laboratory and signed "Melvin A. Miller '46": it is a 1946 drawing, not a photograph, and no photograph of the finished pile on 2 December 1942 is known. Department of Energy record, National Archives 434-RF-62(1) (naId 558600), public domain (PD US DOE on Commons, File:Stagg_Field_reactor.jpg). Saved 1280 x 1004 from the Commons 1280 px thumbnail (original 3000 x 2352); grayscale. Works for the top half spec window: the pile sits centre left with the tower at right. Runner up: the reunion photo of the team on 2 December 1946, the fourth anniversary (Commons File:ChicagoPileTeam.png, Fermi, Zinn, Anderson, Woods, Szilard and others), but Commons gives its source as Los Alamos with an Attribution license, not a clear public domain tag, so check it before any use.

declassified.fact: The scientists named their neutron counters after Winnie the Pooh characters. The instruments watching the world's first chain reaction were called Piglet, Tigger and Pooh.
